conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for making time today. I’m Dr. Ramirez, a perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new mothers. Over the next few minutes I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a brief, well-studied questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during the past seven days.  

Everything we discuss stays between you, me, and the clinical team directly involved in your care, so please feel comfortable answering as honestly as you can. There are only ten questions, and I’ll ask each one conversationally—no need to remember any numbers or categories. If at any point a question feels difficult, we can slow down or pause.  

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:  

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?
Honestly, laughing feels pretty hard lately. My sister sent me a silly meme yesterday and I just… couldn’t muster more than a weak smile. Nothing seems that funny anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really. I might give a little smile if my husband jokes, but it feels forced. Most of the time I’m just too tired or down to find anything truly funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much. I used to get excited about little outings or even just my morning coffee, but lately it all feels kind of flat. I’ll plan things—like taking the baby for a walk—but when the time comes, I’m dragging myself out the door more because I “should” than because I want to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. Yesterday the baby was fussy for an hour straight and I kept thinking it must be something I ate, or that I’m just not soothing him right. My partner says I’m too hard on myself, but I can’t shake the feeling that if I were a better mom, he’d be easier to calm.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting on the couch, baby’s asleep in the bassinet, and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s stopped breathing—so I have to get up and check three or four times. Most of the worry feels like it comes out of nowhere; nothing specific triggered it.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… a few evenings this week I’ve got that sudden wave of panic—like a tight chest, can’t-get-a-full-breath feeling—when I’m just folding laundry. Nothing dangerous is happening, but for a minute it feels like something awful is about to go wrong and I can’t explain why.
Things have been getting on top of me

Mostly I feel I haven’t coped at all. Between the night feeds, the constant laundry, and trying to remember if I ate today, it just piles up. I sit down to rest and immediately think of three other things that need doing; it feels like drowning in small tasks.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with “what-ifs” about the baby, or I replay every little thing I think I did wrong. Some nights I’m still awake an hour after I laid down, and when he cries at 2 a.m. it takes me forever to drift off again.
I have felt sad or miserable
Pretty much every day this week. It’s like there’s a gray cloud hanging over me—even when the baby smiles, the sadness is still right there in the background.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… I’ve cried three or four times since last weekend. Once was when I couldn’t get him to latch, another when I realized I’d forgotten to thaw dinner and we’d have to order take-out again—little things feel like huge failures and the tears just come.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get overwhelmed, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient-reported symptoms (10-item EPDS-style inquiry):

<sym>Depressed mood</sym>: Endorsed daily sadness, frequent crying spells, pervasive “gray cloud” feeling.  
<sym>Anhedonia</sym>: Marked loss of interest/enjoyment; activities done out of obligation.  
<sym>Excessive guilt / self-blame</sym>: Attributes infant fussiness to personal inadequacy.  
<sym>Generalized & perinatal-specific anxiety</sym>: Daily “no-good-reason” worry, repeated infant-breathing checks, panic-like episodes with chest tightness.  
<sym>Sleep disturbance</sym>: Mood-related initial insomnia; difficulty returning to sleep after night feeds.  
<sym>Feeling overwhelmed / unable to cope</sym>: Describes “drowning in small tasks.”  
<sym>Appetite / concentration</sym>: Noted forgetting meals; head “spinning” with intrusive “what-ifs.”

Safety: Denies any self-harm thoughts (Q10 negative).

Pattern: Symptoms present most days × ≥1 week, causing distress and functional impairment; no psychotic features or self-harm ideation identified.

Screening significance:  
- EPDS total consistent with probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety.  
- Meets DSM-5-TR threshold indicators for further evaluation for <med>postpartum depression</med> and <med>generalized anxiety disorder</med>.  
- No emergent safety risks at present.

Recommendation: Refer for comprehensive perinatal mental health assessment; consider standardized EPDS scoring and clinician interview to confirm diagnosis and discuss evidence-based interventions.
